import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The Gerstenhaber problem for three commuting matrices

Gerstenhaber proved in 1961 [Ger61] that the unital algebra generated by two commuting
$n \times n$ matrices over a field has dimension at most $n$. It is an open problem,
known as the **Gerstenhaber problem**, whether the same bound holds for three pairwise
commuting matrices. The bound fails for four or more pairwise commuting matrices.

*References:*
- [Ger61] M. Gerstenhaber, *On dominance and varieties of commuting matrices*.
  Annals of Mathematics (2) 73 (1961), no. 2, 324–348.
  https://doi.org/10.2307/1970336
- [arXiv:2402.16334](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16334), M. Satriano and W. Zhang,
  *On the algebra generated by three commuting matrices: combinatorial cases*.
- [arXiv:2006.08588](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08588), J. Holbrook and M. Omladič,
  *A computing strategy and programs to resolve the Gerstenhaber Problem for
  commuting triples of matrices*.
-/

namespace Gerstenhaber

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] {n : ℕ}

/--
**Gerstenhaber's theorem** [Ger61]: if $A$ and $B$ are commuting $n \times n$
matrices over a field $K$, then the unital $K$-algebra $K[A, B]$ they generate
has dimension at most $n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 15 16]
theorem finrank_adjoin_pair_le (A B : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) K) (hAB : Commute A B) :
    Module.finrank K (Algebra.adjoin K {A, B}) ≤ n := by
  sorry

/--
**The Gerstenhaber problem**: if $A$, $B$, and $C$ are pairwise commuting
$n \times n$ matrices over a field $K$, is the dimension of the unital
$K$-algebra $K[A, B, C]$ they generate always at most $n$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 15 16]
theorem finrank_adjoin_triple_le :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ (K : Type*) [Field K] (n : ℕ) (A B C : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) K),
        ({A, B, C} : Set (Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) K)).Pairwise Commute →
          Module.finrank K (Algebra.adjoin K {A, B, C}) ≤ n := by
  sorry

/--
The analogue of Gerstenhaber's theorem fails for four pairwise commuting matrices:
over any field there are four pairwise commuting $4 \times 4$ matrices generating a unital
algebra of dimension greater than $4$. The standard example is
$e_{13}, e_{14}, e_{23}, e_{24}$, whose pairwise products all vanish, so the algebra
they generate has dimension $5$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 15 16]
theorem exists_finrank_adjoin_quadruple_gt (K : Type*) [Field K] :
    ∃ A B C D : Matrix (Fin 4) (Fin 4) K,
      ({A, B, C, D} : Set (Matrix (Fin 4) (Fin 4) K)).Pairwise Commute ∧
      4 < Module.finrank K (Algebra.adjoin K {A, B, C, D}) := by
  sorry

end Gerstenhaber

findings.description: The reference at lines 31–32 attributes arXiv:2402.16334 to “M. Satriano and W. Zhang.” Its authors are Ron Cherny, Matthew Satriano, and Yohan Song. The URL and title identify the correct paper, and the mathematical statements match it.

reformulations.difference: Lean includes size zero and uses Set.Pairwise Commute rather than spelling out the three commutation equations for positive-size matrices.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Commute is reflexive and symmetric, so {A,B,C}.Pairwise Commute is equivalent to Commute A B ∧ Commute A C ∧ Commute B C, even when matrices coincide. At n=0 the matrix space and every subalgebra are subsingletons, with finrank 0, so the added case satisfies the bound. Review.triple_positive_size_iff in /workspace/review/scratch.lean proves the equivalence of the complete universal statements.

review.notes: No mathematical misformalizations found in any of the three theorems. Both cited arXiv papers explicitly use arbitrary fields and unital generated algebras. All relevant subalgebras are finite-dimensional, so finrank's infinite-dimensional default cannot affect these statements. The scratch file verifies sizes 0 and 1, pairwise-commutation equivalences, and independently proves the exact four-matrix existence theorem over every field. Computable product and linear-independence tests over ZMod 2 returned true; the named proofs contain no sorryAx dependencies. Status tags agree with the retrieved sources. Gerstenhaber's original full text was inaccessible, but its theorem is explicitly restated in both other cited papers and its bibliographic details were checked.
